10	# Browser behaviour, in plain English
11	
12	**In one sentence:** Gitea ships one JavaScript bundle to every page, so the interesting question is
13	not "what does my code do" but "how does it know it is on the right page".
14	**Come here when:** you want something on a page to respond to a click, load data, or show and hide.
15	
16	## What this is
17	
18	All the browser-side code except the Vue components, organised by how reusable it is:
19	
20	- `features/` — one file per page or feature, about eighty of them. This is where most work happens.
21	- `modules/` — shared infrastructure: fetching, initialisation, tooltips, toasts, the code editor.
22	- `utils/` — pure helpers with no assumptions about the page: strings, URLs, dates, colours.
23	- `markup/` and `render/` — enhancing content that has already been rendered.
24	- `webcomponents/` — custom HTML elements like the relative-time display and the `aria-menu` menu button.
25	
26	## Why it exists
27	
28	Gitea builds **one bundle for the whole site**. Every page downloads the same JavaScript.
29	
30	That is a deliberate trade — one file caches well and there is no per-page build — but it creates
31	the central problem this code has to solve. The issue-list code is loaded on the settings page. The
32	diff viewer is loaded on your profile. All of it runs on all of it.
33	
34	So every feature must cheaply determine "am I on a page that needs me?" and get out of the way if
35	not. Everything below follows from that.
36	
37	There is a second problem. Some elements appear *after* the page loads — a comment you just posted,
38	a dropdown rendered on demand. Code that ran once at page load never sees them, which is why the
39	newer of the two wiring mechanisms exists.
40	
41	## Words you'll meet
42	
43	- **bundle** — the single compiled JavaScript file served to every page.
44	- **init function** — a function that sets one feature up.
45	- **early return** — leaving a function immediately when there is nothing to do.
46	- **selector** — a CSS pattern for finding elements, like `.issue-list`.
47	- **data attribute** — a `data-something="value"` attribute on an HTML element.
48	- **observer** — code that watches for elements being added to the page.
49	- **event delegation** — one listener on the document handling clicks on many elements, including
50	  ones added later.
51	- **custom event** — an event your own code invents and dispatches.
52	
53	## What's in these files
54	
55	| Where | What it is for |
56	| --- | --- |
57	| `web_src/js/index.ts` | The entry point. Imports everything and runs the init functions. |
58	| `web_src/js/modules/init.ts` | Runs that list, and can time each entry. |
59	| `web_src/js/modules/observer.ts` | The declarative wiring: the register functions and the observer. |
60	| `web_src/js/modules/fetch.ts` | The HTTP wrappers every request must go through. |
61	| `web_src/js/utils/dom.ts` | Finding elements, showing and hiding them, building them. |
62	| `web_src/js/modules/i18n.ts` | Translated strings on the frontend. |
63	| `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.ts` | Keyboard shortcuts: the list of them, and the `<kbd>` hints beside search boxes. |
64	
65	## The rules, and why
66	
67	### Two ways to wire something up
68	
69	**The old way — page-load init.** Export `initFoo()` from a file in `features/` and add it to the
70	list in `index.ts`. It runs on every page in Gitea, so it **must** look for its elements and return
71	immediately when they are not there.
72	
73	**The new way, and what to prefer.** Register a named function once:
74	`registerGlobalInitFunc('initFoo', (el) => {...})`, then in the template put
75	`data-global-init="initFoo"` on the element. For clicks,
76	`registerGlobalEventFunc('click', 'onFoo', ...)` with `data-global-click="onFoo"`.
77	
78	This is better for two concrete reasons. It runs only when an element that asks for it actually
79	exists — no per-page cost anywhere else. And it also catches elements added to the page later, which
80	the old way cannot. It runs once per element, guarded internally, so a node removed and re-added is
81	not initialised twice.
82	
83	There is a third function that registers by CSS selector. The code that defines it calls it "less
84	efficient and less maintainable" in its own comment. It exists for element types already scattered
85	across many pages. Do not reach for it in new work.
86	
87	**Registration must happen before the observer starts.** `index.ts` deliberately starts the observer
88	last, after everything has registered. Registering afterwards throws an error rather than failing
89	quietly — which is the kind thing for it to do.
90	
91	**One element gets one function.** The attribute is looked up whole, so `data-global-init` names a
92	single function; listing two separated by a space is a TODO in the code, not something that works
93	today. When the element you want already has one — the new-issue title field carries the
94	cursor-positioning behaviour — put your attribute on a wrapper around it and find the inner element
95	from there. Writing two names does at least fail loudly: the whole string is treated as one name,
96	and the lookup throws saying that function was not found.
97	
98	### Everything else
99	
100	**All HTTP goes through the fetch wrappers.** They handle the cross-site request token and error
101	conventions. A raw `fetch` skips both, and will fail on anything that writes.
102	
103	**Show and hide with the helper functions and the hidden class**, not by setting styles directly.
104	Vue components use `v-if` and `v-show` instead — different mechanism, do not mix them.
105	
106	**Read attributes with `getAttribute`, not `dataset`.** The `dataset` property silently renames
107	things: `data-some-value` becomes `someValue`. The rename is invisible and the bug it causes is
108	confusing. And never attach user-provided data to a DOM node.
109	
110	**Custom events are prefixed `ce-`** and declared as an exported constant next to whatever emits
111	them, so the name is defined once instead of typed as a string in two places that can drift apart.
112	
113	**TypeScript conventions:** `import type` for type-only imports, `@ts-expect-error` rather than
114	`@ts-ignore`, `!` rather than `?.` when a value genuinely always exists, and `async` only on
115	functions that actually await something.
116	
117	**One feature per file.** Ids and classes are kebab-case with two or three words naming the feature.
118	
119	## How to actually do it
120	
121	**Make an element do something.** Register a global init function in the relevant `features/` file
122	and add `data-global-init="yourFuncName"` to the element in its template. No change to `index.ts`.
123	
124	**Add a whole-page feature.** Create `features/<name>.ts` exporting `initName()`. Find your root
125	element first and **return immediately if it is missing**. Then add the import and the list entry in
126	`index.ts`.
127	
128	**Find out why a page feels slow.** Add `?_ui_performance_trace=1` to the URL and the timings for
129	every init function are printed. `index.ts` already logs an error if the total exceeds 500ms.
130	
131	**Add a keyboard shortcut.** Call `registerShortcut` (`modules/shortcut.ts`); keys `g c` mean `g`
132	then `c`. Tie it to an element and it lasts only while that element is on the page, even if hidden.
133	Two live shortcuts that clash throw at once, instead of one quietly winning.
134	
135	**Run one test file.** `pnpm exec vitest <path-filter>`.
136	
137	**Show an issue for a number someone typed.** Reuse `matchIssue` (`utils/match.ts`), the search
138	behind the `#` list. It puts the issue with that exact number first and leaves out the one you're
139	on, as the duplicate close reason's preview does. Only its word matches are limited to what the
140	viewer may read: the item with the typed number comes back even when it's a pull request the viewer
141	can't open.
142	
143	## Traps, and what they look like
144	
145	**The whole site gets slower after your change.** You added a page-load init without an early
146	return, so your feature's setup cost is now paid on every page in Gitea. The 500ms warning in the
147	console exists to catch exactly this.
148	
149	**Your code works on load and not on new elements.** A comment posted without a page reload does not
150	get your behaviour. You used page-load init; use the declarative mechanism, which sees them.
151	
152	**Your `data-` attribute reads as undefined.** You used `dataset` and the property name was
153	silently camel-cased. Use `getAttribute` with the literal attribute name.
154	
155	**Your request is rejected, usually as a 403.** You used a raw `fetch` and skipped the wrappers,
156	which is what adds the request token.
157	
158	**Registering a global init function throws.** You registered it after the observer started.
159	Registration happens at module load; the observer starts last, on purpose.
160	
161	**You build on Fomantic-UI because the existing code does.** It is the vendored jQuery library, and
162	it is deprecated. Do not start new features on it, and never mix its JavaScript with Vue — Vue may
163	use its CSS classes, but the two fight over who owns the DOM.
164	For a plain menu of actions there is a newer `<aria-menu>` element (`web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu.ts`);
165	`web_src/js/modules/fomantic/aria.md` explains when to pick it over a Fomantic dropdown.
166	
167	**You put a helper in `utils/` and it breaks in tests.** That folder is for pure helpers. Anything
168	reaching for `window` or searching the page belongs in `modules/` or `features/`.
169	
170	**Your feature crashes when it asks the comment box what was typed.** A feature can follow a
171	comment box someone else set up: the box's "content changed" and "upload" events travel up the
172	page (`features/comp/EditorMarkdown.ts`, `features/comp/EditorUpload.ts`), and
173	`getComboMarkdownEditor` hands you the editor, as `features/repo-issue-status-button.ts` does. The
174	catch is timing: the editor is attached to its box *before* it finishes setting up, so asking it
175	anything too early throws. Read the box's textarea at start-up, and only ask the editor once one of
176	its events arrives — the events come from an editor that is ready.
177	
178	**Your menu works with the mouse but not with the keyboard.** You listened for clicks on the items
179	of a Fomantic dropdown. Pressing Enter on a highlighted item only becomes a real click when the item
180	is a link or has the class `js-aria-clickable` — Gitea's own patch in
181	`web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts` does that, so everything else is handled inside Fomantic
182	and your listener never hears it. Add the class, as the close reason menu
183	(`templates/repo/issue/view_content.tmpl`) does. An `<aria-menu>` needs none of this: Enter and
184	Space on one of its items call the item's own `click()`, so a plain click listener hears both.
185	
186	**You focus a box after a menu pick, and the focus jumps back.** When an item of a Fomantic dropdown
187	is clicked, the dropdown puts the focus back on itself after your click handler has run. Wait one
188	tick with `setTimeout(..., 0)` before focusing anything else.
189	
190	**The values typed in your popup never reach the server.** `createTippy` (`modules/tippy.ts`)
191	moves a popup's content to the end of the page while it is shown, so any input inside it is no
192	longer inside its `<form>` and the form does not send it. Copy the value into a hidden field that
193	stays in the form, as the close reason popups in `features/repo-issue-status-button.ts` do.
194	
195	## Where to go next
196	
197	- `docs/frontend-js.md` (in this folder) — the reference page this was written from
198	- `frontend-vue-components.md` — when a feature is complex enough to deserve Vue
199	- `templates.md` — where those `data-global-init` attributes are written
200	- `frontend-css.md` — the hidden class and the naming conventions

11	## Responsibilities
12	
13	| Directory | Owns |
14	| --- | --- |
15	| `features/` | one file per page or feature (`repo-issue.ts`, `repo-diff.ts`, `repo-code.ts`), plus `features/admin/` and `features/comp/` for shared widgets |

17	| `utils/` | pure helpers with no DOM assumptions: `dom.ts`, `html.ts`, `url.ts`, `time.ts`, `color.ts`, `string.ts` |
18	| `markup/`, `render/` | enhancing already-rendered content (anchors, mermaid, math) |

22	
23	| Path | What it holds |

32	
33	## Conventions & invariants
34	
35	**Two ways to wire a feature, and new code should prefer the second.**
36	
37	1. *Page-load init:* export `initFoo()` from a `features/` file and add it to the array in
38	   `index.ts`. Every function in that array runs on **every** page, so it must find its elements
39	   and return immediately when they are absent.
40	2. *Declarative:* `registerGlobalInitFunc('initFoo', (el) => {...})` in the module, and
41	   `data-global-init="initFoo"` on the element in the template. For clicks,
42	   `registerGlobalEventFunc('click', 'onFoo', ...)` with `data-global-click="onFoo"`. This covers
43	   elements added to the DOM later and runs once per element (guarded by an internal
44	   `_giteaGlobalInited` flag), so re-adding a node does not re-initialise it.
45	
46	`registerGlobalSelectorFunc(selector, handler)` also exists, but `observer.ts` marks it as "less
47	efficient and less maintainable" — it is for element types already on many pages, not new work.
48	
49	- **Ordering rule:** every `registerGlobalInitFunc` must run *before* `initGlobalSelectorObserver`,
50	  which `index.ts` deliberately calls last. Registering after it throws.
51	- **One function per element.** `callGlobalInitFunc` in `observer.ts` looks the attribute up as a
52	  whole string, so `data-global-init` names exactly one function — space-separating two is an open
53	  TODO there, not a feature. To add behaviour to an element that already has one (the new-issue
54	  title in `templates/repo/issue/new_form.tmpl` carries `autoFocusEnd`), put the attribute on a
55	  wrapper and query for the inner element.
56	- Data fetching goes through the `fetch.ts` wrappers, never a raw `fetch`.
57	- Show and hide with `.tw-hidden` plus `showElem` / `hideElem` / `toggleElem`. In Vue use
58	  `v-if`/`v-show` instead (`frontend-vue-components.md`).
59	- Use `node.getAttribute`, not `node.dataset` (camel-casing surprises), and never bind
60	  user-provided data onto a DOM node.
61	- Custom DOM events are prefixed `ce-`, declared as an exported constant next to their emitter —
62	  see `EventEditorContentChanged` in `features/comp/EditorMarkdown.ts`.
63	- TypeScript, per `docs/guidelines-frontend.md`: `import type` for type-only imports,
64	  `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`, `!` rather than `?.`/`??` when a value always exists, and
65	  `async` only on a function that actually awaits.
66	- One feature per file or directory; ids and classes are kebab-case with 2-3 feature keywords.
67	
68	## Recipes
69	
70	**Add behaviour to an element.** Register a global init func in the owning `features/` module and
71	put `data-global-init="yourFuncName"` on the element in its template. No change to `index.ts`.
72	
73	**Add a whole-page feature.** New `features/<name>.ts` exporting `initName()`, an early return when
74	its root element is missing, then add the import and the array entry in `index.ts`.
75	
76	**Profile a slow page.** Append `?_ui_performance_trace=1` to the URL to print per-init timings.
77	`index.ts` already logs an error when total init exceeds 500ms.
78	
79	**Look up an issue by its number.** `matchIssue` (`utils/match.ts`) is the `#` list's search: a
80	number comes back first (`services/issue/suggestion.go` → `GetSuggestion`), and the current issue
81	is left out. Keyword matches are limited to the kinds the viewer may read
82	(`routers/web/repo/issue_suggestions.go`), but the match by number (`GetIssueByIndex`) is not, so a
83	viewer who can't read pull requests still gets one typed by its number. The duplicate close
84	reason's preview in `features/repo-issue-status-button.ts` uses it.
85	
86	**Add a keyboard shortcut.** Call `registerShortcut` (`modules/shortcut.ts`). One given an `element`
87	exists while that element is in the document, hidden or not; a clash with a live one throws. For
88	one that goes where a link goes, mark the link instead: `data-global-init="onShortcutLink"`,
89	`data-shortcut-keys`, `data-shortcut-description` (the link's text may hold a count) and optionally
90	`data-shortcut-section`, plus `data-shortcut-href` to go somewhere other than its `href`, as the
91	Code tab's `g c` does (`templates/repo/header.tmpl`). The shortcut then exists exactly when the
92	template renders the link. Markup a page renders twice, such as the navbar icons for the phone and
93	desktop layouts (`templates/base/head_navbar.tmpl`), must mark one copy only.
94	
95	**Run one test file.** `pnpm exec vitest <path-filter>` (`testing.md`).
96	
97	## Gotchas
98	
99	- Forgetting the early return in a page-load init means that feature's cost is paid on every page
100	  in Gitea, which is what the 500ms warning is there to catch.
101	- Fomantic-UI (jQuery) is vendored and deprecated. Do not build new features on it, and do not mix
102	  it with Vue — Vue may use its CSS classes but not its JavaScript.
103	- Which menu to build on, Fomantic dropdown or `<aria-menu>` (`web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu.ts`),
104	  is decided in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/aria.md`.
105	- `utils/` is for pure helpers. A function that reaches for `window` or a global selector belongs
106	  in `modules/` or `features/`.
107	- A feature can follow a comment box it did not create: the editor's change and upload events
108	  bubble (`features/comp/EditorMarkdown.ts`, `features/comp/EditorUpload.ts`), and
109	  `getComboMarkdownEditor` finds the editor, as `features/repo-issue-status-button.ts` does. But
110	  the editor attaches itself before its async `init` finishes, and calling it before then throws;
111	  read its textarea until an event arrives.
112	- Enter on a Fomantic dropdown item only fires a `click` when the item is a link or carries
113	  `js-aria-clickable` (`web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts`), so a plain click listener on other
114	  items never hears a keyboard pick. The close reason menu in `templates/repo/issue/view_content.tmpl`
115	  marks its items; an `<aria-menu>` item needs no class, as Enter and Space call its `click()`.
116	- After a click on a Fomantic dropdown item, the dropdown keeps the focus, so focusing something
117	  else from your click handler needs `setTimeout(..., 0)`.
118	- `createTippy` (`modules/tippy.ts`) moves a popup to `document.body`, so inputs in it leave their
119	  `<form>` and are not sent. Keep their values in hidden fields inside the form, as the close reason
120	  popups in `features/repo-issue-status-button.ts` do.

# AI assistance disclosure — required format

Course rule, not an upstream Gitea one. Every contributor discloses their own AI use per issue,
**even when no AI was used**. Source: the course AI Log Instructions page and `CONTRIBUTING.md`
(AI Contribution Policy). Two separate places, both required. The rest of the PR and issue
format is in `COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.

## 1. A comment on the issue

Posted by each contributor on the **issue** they worked, once their work is done. One comment per
person — never edit someone else's. Add later sessions by editing your own table.

```markdown
### AI Assistance — @your-github-username

**Role in this issue:** Implementation

| # | Tool | Log | What AI helped with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | claude-code | [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/blob/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md) | Confirmed the files found during concept location, drafted the template change and tests, ran them |

**Attachments:** [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl/](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/tree/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl)
```

- **Role** is one of Implementation, Code review, Testing, Other — pick the ones that apply and
  delete the rest, do not leave the slash list in place.
- **Tool** is the tool's name, e.g. `claude-code`, `claude-web`.
- **Log** is a full `https://github.com/...` link to the filed log. Relative paths break in issue
  comments. File naming is in `ai-logs/README.md`.
- **Attachments** only when the log has a companion folder; otherwise drop the line.
- **No AI used?** Keep the heading and role line and write `No AI used` in place of the table.

## 2. A short section in the pull request description — no log link

Reviewers read the PR, and the review rubric scores "AI transparency", so the PR says how AI was
used and how you verified it. It does **not** link or cite the AI log: from Sprint 1 on, logs are
referenced in **issue comments only**, never in PR descriptions or PR comments (Sprint 1 page, D5).

```markdown
## AI assistance

Claude Code (claude-opus-5) drafted the handler and tests following the existing register/delete
code; I reviewed every line, ran the tests, checked the page by hand, and can explain each change.
AI log: see the AI Assistance comment on the linked issue.
```

Name the model, say what AI did and what you did, and point at the issue comment for the log.

## Rules that make a disclosure wrong

- **Placeholders left in**: `@your-github-username` or the full `Implementation / Code review /
  Testing / Other` list means the comment was pasted unread.
- **A log link in a PR description or PR comment.** Log links live in the issue comment only.
- **A log link that 404s.** Until the log is merged to `main`, link the branch that holds it; switch
  to the `main` link once merged.
- **A log folder that is not your GitHub username** — `ai-logs/sprint1/jdonohue/` is wrong when the
  account is `Jack-Donohue`.
- **Claiming work AI did as your own, or the reverse.** The claim must match the log.
- **AI-written replies to reviewer questions on your own issue or PR.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` forbids it:
  the questions are for you.

## For AI agents drafting an issue or PR

Put section 2 in every PR description you draft, and draft the section 1 issue comment
separately, both filled in from the session you actually ran — never with placeholders. You may
draft the wording, but say plainly that the human must review and edit it before posting, and leave
the issue comment for them to post under their own account.
```

Title: feat(shortcut): g shortcuts for the repository tabs and notifications

Closes #58

## What changed and why

GitHub users move around a repository with two-key `g` shortcuts, and Gitea had none. Building on #56's registry, this PR adds them: `g c`, `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` go to a repository's Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions and Wiki tabs, and `g n` goes to the user's notifications from any page.

- **A link can declare its own shortcut.** A link in a template that carries a few attributes registers a shortcut that goes where the link leads. The shortcut only exists while the link is on the page, so it follows whatever the template already decides about the link.
- **The tab bar declares the repository shortcuts.** Each tab marks itself, so a tab that isn't shown (its feature is turned off, the user can't read it, or it is Actions on an empty repository) has no shortcut. The external issue tracker and external wiki tabs aren't marked, so a shortcut never leaves Gitea. Tabs that move into the "more" menu on a narrow window are still on the page, so their shortcuts keep working.
- **`g c` goes to the repository's front page,** not where the Code tab links: on a branch other than the default, the Code tab points at that branch.
- **`g n` is declared on the notifications bell,** which only signed-in users have. The bell is in the page twice, once for phones and once for desktops, so only one copy declares it.
- **Each shortcut is listed with its tab's translated name** ("Issues", without the open count), in the "Repository" section with `s` and `t`. `g n` is "Notifications" under a new "General" string, which #57's help dialog will also use for `?`.
- The docs in `.claude-students` are updated with the new way to add a shortcut.

## How the changes relate to the ACs

- **AC1:** `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` on a repository page go to that tab.
- **AC2:** `g c` goes to the repository's front page on the default branch, even while browsing another branch.
- **AC3:** a tab that is not shown declares no shortcut, so its keys do nothing.
- **AC4:** the external tracker and wiki tabs declare no shortcut, so `g i` and `g w` do nothing there and the browser stays in Gitea.
- **AC5:** tabs in the "more" menu are still on the page, so their shortcuts work.
- **AC6:** signed in, `g n` goes to notifications from any page; signed out there is no bell, so it does nothing.
- **AC7:** outside a repository there is no tab bar, so the repository shortcuts do nothing.
- **AC8:** each repository shortcut has its tab's name in the Repository section, and `g n` is "Notifications" under "General".

## How it was tested

### Test strategy

- **Unit tests (Vitest) for the link shortcut.** 4 new tests in `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.test.ts` check that a link's shortcut goes where the link leads, or to its own address when it has one (`g c`), that it keeps working after the link moves into a hidden part of the page as the "more" menu does, and that it is listed with its own description instead of the link's text. They are named `#58 AC…`, because the other tests in that file use #56's AC numbers.
- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** Which tabs exist, the "more" menu and the bell are decided by Gitea's templates and the page at runtime, which a unit test can't reach. 4 new tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` drive real pages: every tab shortcut, including `g c` from another branch (AC1, AC2, AC8); a repository with pull requests and Actions turned off and an external tracker and wiki (AC3, AC4); a narrow window (AC5); and `g n` signed out and signed in, outside a repository (AC6, AC7, AC8). A new `apiEditRepo` helper in `tests/e2e/utils.ts` turns those units off.

**Testing the tests.** Each test was checked by breaking the code it guards and confirming it fails. For the unit tests: taking the description from the link's text, dropping the section, an action that does nothing, ignoring a link's own address, and treating a hidden part of the page as gone. For the Playwright tests: the Code tab without its own address, a shortcut on the external tracker tab, both bells declaring `g n`, and treating hidden elements as gone. Each break failed the matching tests, and #56's tests stayed green.

**Not covered automatically, and why.** AC3's other cases, a tab the user can't read and Actions on an empty repository, aren't driven separately. The template hides those tabs the same way it hides a turned-off one, which the AC3 test covers.

**Checked by hand.** Claude also drove a headless browser through a local instance: the tab shortcuts, `g c` from a branch, a narrow window, and `g n` signed in and out.

| AC | What the tests check |
| --- | --- |
| AC1 | `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` each go to their tab on a real repository; a link's shortcut goes where the link leads |
| AC2 | On a branch other than the default, the Code tab links to that branch and `g c` goes to the front page; a link's shortcut can go to its own address |
| AC3 | With pull requests and Actions turned off, no `g p` or `g a` is declared, the keys do nothing and a live shortcut still runs after them |
| AC4 | With an external tracker and wiki, their tabs are shown but declare nothing, the keys do nothing and no new tab opens |
| AC5 | At 420 px wide the Wiki tab is in the "more" menu and `g w` still works; a link moved into a hidden part of the page keeps its shortcut |
| AC6 | Signed out there is no `g n`; signed in there is exactly one, and it goes to notifications |
| AC7 | On `/explore/repos` no repository shortcut is declared |
| AC8 | Issues is "Issues" in "Repository", and `g n` is "Notifications" in "General"; a link is listed with its own description, not its text |

## CI / manual verification

- CI runs on the PR; per the course rules, it must pass before merging.
- `make test-frontend`: 360 tests pass, including the 4 new ones.
- `make lint-js`, `make lint-templates`, `make lint-editorconfig` and the locale JSON lint pass.
- The 7 Playwright tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` pass locally on Chromium and Firefox; each new one runs in under 1.5 s.
- `./.claude-students/check.sh` reports only the two `models-issues.md` size limits, which were failing before this PR.

## Design

Design decisions noted under issue #58.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- `g n` and the tabs in the "more" menu rely on #56 counting a hidden element as present. The bell that declares `g n` is the phone-layout copy, which is hidden on desktops, and tabs in the closed "more" menu are hidden too. If the registry ever started ignoring hidden elements, as #56's Tech Debt suggests later shortcuts might need, both would stop working. The Playwright tests for AC5 and AC6 fail if that happens.

**Encountered:**
- The navbar renders its icons, the notifications bell among them, twice: once for the phone layout and once for desktop, with CSS hiding one. Both copies are always in the page, so marking both with `g n` makes #56's registry throw a clash on every page for signed-in users. Handled by a `WithShortcut` flag that only the copy rendered for every signed-in user passes. The core issue of two notification bells was not fixed here.

Keep this summary up-to-date as the PR evolves. \
If your PR changes the UI, you must add **after** screenshots in the PR summary. \
If you are not implementing a new feature, you should also post **before** screenshots for comparison.

If you are implementing a new feature, your PR will only be merged if your screenshots are up to date.\
Furthermore, feature PRs will only be merged if their summary contains a clear usage description (understandable for users) and testing description (understandable for reviewers).
You should strive to combine both into a single description.

Another requirement for merging PRs is that the PR is labeled correctly.\
- A PR is opened from its issue branch into main, and main is protected, so every change goes through a PR.
- The PR title follows Conventional Commits, and the description is written in your own words, explaining
  what changed and why.
- Follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the description: features include how to use them and how they were tested,
  UI changes include screenshots, and each closed issue is listed as `Closes #<N>` on its own line.
- Add a short note on how AI was used (see AI tool use).
- Keep the PR as a draft while working on it, then mark it ready for review and request a reviewer.

 `./.specstory/issue-58-pr-description.md`

```text
1	Title: feat(shortcut): g shortcuts for the repository tabs and notifications
2	
3	Closes #58
4	
5	## What changed and why
6	
7	GitHub users move around a repository with two-key `g` shortcuts, and Gitea had none. Building on #56's registry, this PR adds them: `g c`, `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` go to a repository's Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions and Wiki tabs, and `g n` goes to the user's notifications from any page.
8	
9	- **A link can declare its own shortcut.** A link in a template that carries a few attributes registers a shortcut that goes where the link leads. The shortcut only exists while the link is on the page, so it follows whatever the template already decides about the link.
10	- **The tab bar declares the repository shortcuts.** Each tab marks itself, so a tab that isn't shown (its feature is turned off, the user can't read it, or it is Actions on an empty repository) has no shortcut. Tabs that move into the "more" menu on a narrow window are still on the page, so their shortcuts keep working.

## How it was tested

### Test strategy

Most of the risk in this PR is in the wiring, not the code: whether a shortcut exists is decided by the templates, so most mistakes only show up on a real page. The tests are split along that line.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

  updateItems = throttle(100, () => {
    if (!this.popup) {
      const div = document.createElement('div');
      div.classList.add('overflow-menu-popup');
      div.setAttribute('role', 'menu');
      div.tabIndex = -1; // for initial focus, programmatic focus only
      div.style.display = 'none';
      div.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => {
        if (e.isComposing) return;
        if (e.key === 'Tab') {
          const items = this.popup.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('[role="menuitem"]');
          if (e.shiftKey) {
            if (document.activeElement === items[0]) {
              e.preventDefault();
              items[items.length - 1].focus();
            }
          } else {
            if (document.activeElement === items[items.length - 1]) {
              e.preventDefault();
              items[0].focus();
            }
      this.handleItemClick(div, '.overflow-menu-popup > .item');
      this.popup = div;
    } // end if: no popup and create a new one

    const itemFlexSpace = this.menuItemsEl.querySelector<HTMLSpanElement>('.item-flex-space');
    const itemOverFlowMenuButton = this.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('.overflow-menu-button');

    // move items in popup back into the menu items for subsequent measurement
    for (const item of this.overflowItems) {
      if (!itemFlexSpace || item.getAttribute('data-after-flex-space')) {
        this.menuItemsEl.append(item);
      } else {
        itemFlexSpace.insertAdjacentElement('beforebegin', item);
      }
    }

    // measure which items are partially outside the element and move them into the button menu
    // flex space and overflow menu are excluded from measurement
    itemFlexSpace?.style.setProperty('display', 'none', 'important');
    itemOverFlowMenuButton?.style.setProperty('display', 'none', 'important');
    this.overflowItems = [];
    const menuRight = this.offsetLeft + this.offsetWidth;
    const menuItems = this.menuItemsEl.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('.item, .item-flex-space');
    let afterFlexSpace = false;
    for (const [idx, item] of menuItems.entries()) {
      if (item.classList.contains('item-flex-space')) {
        afterFlexSpace = true;
        continue;
      }
      if (afterFlexSpace) item.setAttribute('data-after-flex-space', 'true');
      const itemRight = item.offsetLeft + item.offsetWidth;
      if (menuRight - itemRight < 38) { // roughly the width of .overflow-menu-button with some extra space
        const onlyLastItem = idx === menuItems.length - 1 && this.overflowItems.length === 0;
        const lastItemFit = onlyLastItem && menuRight > itemRight;
        const moveToPopup = !onlyLastItem || !lastItemFit;
        if (moveToPopup) this.overflowItems.push(item);
      }
    }
    itemFlexSpace?.style.removeProperty('display');
    itemOverFlowMenuButton?.style.removeProperty('display');

    // if there are no overflown items, remove any previously created button
    if (!this.overflowItems?.length) {
      this.hidePopup();
      this.button?.remove();
      this.popup?.remove();
      this.button = null;
      return;
    }

    // remove aria role from items that moved from popup to menu
    for (const item of menuItems) {
      if (!this.overflowItems.includes(item)) {
        item.removeAttribute('role');
      }
    }

    // move all items that overflow into popup
    for (const item of this.overflowItems) {
      item.setAttribute('role', 'menuitem');
      this.popup.append(item);
    }

    // update existing popup
    if (this.button) {
      this.updateButtonActivationState();
      return;
    }

    // create button and attach popup
    const popupId = generateElemId('overflow-popup-');
    this.popup.id = popupId;

    this.button = document.createElement('button');
    this.button.classList.add('overflow-menu-button');
    this.button.setAttribute('aria-label', window.config.i18n.more_items);
    this.button.setAttribute('aria-haspopup', 'true');
    this.button.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
    this.button.setAttribute('aria-controls', popupId);
    this.button.innerHTML = octiconKebabHorizontal;
    this.button.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
      e.stopPropagation();
      if (this.popup.style.display === 'none') {
        this.showPopup();
      } else {
        this.hidePopup();
      }
    });
    this.append(this.button);
    this.append(this.popup);
    this.updateButtonActivationState();
  });

import {env} from 'node:process';
import {test, expect} from '@playwright/test';
import type {Page} from '@playwright/test';
import {apiCreateBranch, apiCreateFile, apiCreateRepo, apiEditRepo, assertNoJsError, login, randomString} from './utils.ts';

async function createRepo(page: Page) {
  const repoName = `e2e-shortcut-${randomString(8)}`;
  await apiCreateRepo(page.request, {name: repoName});
  await apiCreateFile(page.request, env.GITEA_TEST_E2E_USER, repoName, 'other.txt', 'other file');
  return `/${env.GITEA_TEST_E2E_USER}/${repoName}`;
}

// presses a shortcut that leaves the page, and waits until the next page can take one
async function goWith(page: Page, keys: string, url: RegExp) {
  for (const key of keys.split(' ')) await page.keyboard.press(key);
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(url);
  await page.waitForLoadState();
}

test('s and t focus their boxes, and Escape clears them', async ({page}) => {
  await page.goto(await createRepo(page));
  const search = page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top input[name="q"]');
  const searchHint = page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top kbd');
  const goToFile = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container input');
  const goToFileHint = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container kbd');
  await expect(goToFileHint).toHaveAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', 't'); // the Vue box has mounted and registered
  await expect(searchHint).toHaveAttribute('data-shortcut-section', 'Repository');
  await expect(goToFileHint).toHaveAttribute('data-shortcut-section', 'Repository');

  await page.keyboard.press('s');
  await expect(search).toBeFocused();
  await expect(searchHint).toBeHidden();
  await page.keyboard.type('st');
  await expect(search).toHaveValue('st');
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');

test('a key the language menu uses for type-ahead runs no shortcut', async ({page}) => {
  await page.goto(await createRepo(page));
  await expect(page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top kbd')).toHaveAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', 's'); // s is a live shortcut here
  await page.locator('aria-menu:has(.language-menu) > button').focus();
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  await page.keyboard.press('s'); // jumps to a language starting with "s", such as Suomi
  await expect(page.locator('.language-menu .item:focus')).toHaveText(/^s/i);
  await expect(page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top input[name="q"]')).not.toBeFocused();
  await assertNoJsError(page);
});

test('t keeps working after moving through the file tree', async ({page}) => {
  const repoLink = await createRepo(page);
  await page.goto(`${repoLink}/src/branch/main/README.md`); // the file tree is shown by default
  const goToFile = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container input');
  const goToFileHint = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container kbd');

  for (const [file, content] of [['other.txt', 'other file'], ['README.md', 'e2e-shortcut-']]) {
    await page.locator(`#view-file-tree .tree-item[title="${file}"]`).click();
    await expect(page.locator('.file-view')).toContainText(content); // the page content was swapped
    await expect(goToFileHint).toHaveAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', 't'); // the new hint has registered
    await page.keyboard.press('t');
    await expect(goToFile).toBeFocused();
    await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  }

  });

  init() {
    // for horizontal menus where fomantic boldens active items, prevent this bold text from
    // enlarging the menu's active item replacing the text node with a div that renders a
    // invisible pseudo-element that enlarges the box.
    if (this.matches('.ui.secondary.pointing.menu, .ui.tabular.menu')) {
      for (const item of this.querySelectorAll('.item')) {
        for (const child of item.childNodes) {
          if (child.nodeType === Node.TEXT_NODE) {
            const text = child.textContent?.trim(); // whitespace is insignificant inside flexbox
            if (!text) continue;
            const span = document.createElement('span');
            span.classList.add('resize-for-semibold');
            span.setAttribute('data-text', text);
            span.textContent = text;
            child.replaceWith(span);
          }
        }
      }
    }

    // ResizeObserver triggers on initial render, so we don't manually call `updateItems` here which
    // also avoids a full-page FOUC in Firefox that happens when `updateItems` is called too soon.
    this.resizeObserver = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
      for (const entry of entries) {
        const newWidth = entry.contentBoxSize[0].inlineSize;
        if (newWidth !== this.lastWidth) {
          requestAnimationFrame(() => {
            this.updateItems();
          });
          this.lastWidth = newWidth;
        }
      }
    });
    this.resizeObserver.observe(this);
    this.handleItemClick(this, '.overflow-menu-items > .item');
  }

  handleItemClick(el: Element, selector: string) {
    addDelegatedEventListener(el, 'click', selector, () => {

      this.updateButtonActivationState();
    });

  connectedCallback() {
    this.setAttribute('role', 'navigation');

    // check whether the mandatory `.overflow-menu-items` element is present initially which happens
    // with Vue which renders differently than browsers. If it's not there, like in the case of browser
    // template rendering, wait for its addition.
    // The eslint rule is not sophisticated enough or aware of this problem, see
    // https://github.com/43081j/eslint-plugin-wc/pull/130
    const menuItemsEl = this.querySelector<HTMLElement>('.overflow-menu-items'); // eslint-disable-line wc/no-child-traversal-in-connectedcallback
    if (menuItemsEl) {
      this.menuItemsEl = menuItemsEl;
      this.init();
    } else {
      this.mutationObserver = new MutationObserver((mutations) => {
        for (const mutation of mutations) {
          for (const node of mutation.addedNodes as NodeListOf<HTMLElement>) {
            if (!isDocumentFragmentOrElementNode(node)) continue;
            if (node.classList.contains('overflow-menu-items')) {
              this.menuItemsEl = node;
              this.mutationObserver?.disconnect();
              this.init();
            }
          }
        }
      });
      this.mutationObserver.observe(this, {childList: true});
    }
  }

      this.handleBlur = () => this.container.classList.remove('cm-mod-held');
      document.addEventListener('keydown', this.handleKeyDown);
      document.addEventListener('keyup', this.handleKeyUp);
      window.addEventListener('blur', this.handleBlur);
    }
    destroy() {
      document.removeEventListener('keydown', this.handleKeyDown);
      document.removeEventListener('keyup', this.handleKeyUp);
      window.removeEventListener('blur', this.handleBlur);
      this.container.classList.remove('cm-mod-held');
    }
  });

  return [plugin, handler, modClass];

    if (e.isComposing) return;
    const items = this.items();
    const current = items.indexOf(e.target as HTMLElement);
    if (e.key === 'Tab') {
      // focus the trigger and let the default action move on from there
      this.close(true);
      return;
    }
    if (e.key === 'Escape') {
      e.stopPropagation(); // don't also close a surrounding modal
      this.close(true);
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') {
      items[(current + 1) % items.length].focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') {
      items.at(current <= 0 ? -1 : current - 1)!.focus();

      items[0].focus();

      this.focusByFirstChar(items, current, e.key);
    } else {

```text
   79 issue-58-pr-description.md
   17 decisions.md
   96 total
     1	Title: feat(shortcut): g shortcuts for the repository tabs and notifications
     2	
     3	Closes #58
     4	
     5	## What changed and why
     6	
     7	GitHub users move around a repository with two-key `g` shortcuts, and Gitea had none. Building on #56's registry, this PR adds them: `g c`, `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` go to a repository's Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions and Wiki tabs, and `g n` goes to the user's notifications from any page.
     8	
     9	- **A link can declare its own shortcut.** A link in a template that carries a few attributes registers a shortcut that goes where the link leads. The shortcut only exists while the link is on the page, so it follows whatever the template already decides about the link.
    10	- **The tab bar declares the repository shortcuts.** Each tab marks itself, so a tab that isn't shown (its feature is turned off, the user can't read it, or it is Actions on an empty repository) has no shortcut. The external issue tracker and external wiki tabs aren't marked, so a shortcut never leaves Gitea. Tabs that move into the "more" menu on a narrow window are still on the page, so their shortcuts keep working.
    11	- **`g c` goes to the repository's front page,** not where the Code tab links: on a branch other than the default, the Code tab points at that branch.
    12	- **`g n` is declared on the notifications bell,** which only signed-in users have. The bell is in the page twice, once for phones and once for desktops, so only one copy declares it.
    13	- **Each shortcut is listed with its tab's translated name** ("Issues", without the open count), in the "Repository" section with `s` and `t`. `g n` is "Notifications" under a new "General" string, which #57's help dialog will also use for `?`.
    14	- The docs in `.claude-students` are updated with the new way to add a shortcut.
    15	
    16	## How the changes relate to the ACs
    17	
    18	- **AC1:** `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` on a repository page go to that tab.
    19	- **AC2:** `g c` goes to the repository's front page on the default branch, even while browsing another branch.
    20	- **AC3:** a tab that is not shown declares no shortcut, so its keys do nothing.
    21	- **AC4:** the external tracker and wiki tabs declare no shortcut, so `g i` and `g w` do nothing there and the browser stays in Gitea.
    22	- **AC5:** tabs in the "more" menu are still on the page, so their shortcuts work.
    23	- **AC6:** signed in, `g n` goes to notifications from any page; signed out there is no bell, so it does nothing.
    24	- **AC7:** outside a repository there is no tab bar, so the repository shortcuts do nothing.
    25	- **AC8:** each repository shortcut has its tab's name in the Repository section, and `g n` is "Notifications" under "General".
    26	
    27	## How it was tested
    28	
    29	### Test strategy
    30	
    31	Most of the risk in this PR is in the wiring, not the code: whether a shortcut exists is decided by the templates, so most mistakes only show up on a real page. The tests are split along that line.
    32	
    33	- **Unit tests (Vitest) for the part that is plain code.** Turning a link into a shortcut needs no server, so it is tested on its own, where the tests are fast and a failure points straight at the cause. The 4 new tests in `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.test.ts` target the three places where the obvious version would be wrong: a description taken from the link's text would include the open count, following the link would keep `g c` on the browsed branch, and treating a hidden link as gone would break the "more" menu. They are named `#58 AC…`, because the other tests in that file use #56's AC numbers.
    34	- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** A unit test can't see which tabs a template renders. Each of the 4 new tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` sets up the one situation where a wiring mistake would show: a branch other than the default, the only time `g c` and the Code tab disagree; turned-off and external tabs, the only time a shortcut could outlive its tab or leave Gitea; a narrow window, the only time tabs move; and a signed-in user, the only time there are two bells to clash. On an ordinary page each of these mistakes would pass unnoticed. A new `apiEditRepo` helper in `tests/e2e/utils.ts` sets up the repository with the turned-off and external tabs.
    35	- **Proving that nothing happened.** A test that presses a dead shortcut and sees nothing would also pass on a page where no key works at all. The AC3 and AC4 test therefore presses a live shortcut (`s`) after the dead ones and checks that it still runs.
    36	
    37	**Testing the tests.** Each test was checked via mutation testing to ensure that the tests actually detect something real. ```text
     1	## Design Decisions - @ab-wm
     2	
     3	### Decisions for Commit 1
     4	#### Decision 1: Each tab's link in the tab bar declares its own `g` shortcut
     5	
     6	**Decision:** The tab bar's links declare their shortcuts in the page's HTML, and a shortcut goes where its link leads. The one exception is `g c`, which goes to the repository's front page instead of the branch the Code tab points at. The notifications bell declares `g n` the same way.
     7	**Alternatives Considered:** (a) The server works out which tabs the user may open and hands the page a list of their addresses. (b) The page code builds each address from the repository's address, for example by adding `/issues`.
     8	**Rationale:** The tab bar already decides which tabs to show. It leaves out a tab whose feature is turned off, one the user cannot read, and Actions on an empty repository, and it shows an outside link for an external tracker or wiki. Declaring the shortcut on the tab means a shortcut exists exactly when its tab does, so AC3, AC4 and AC7 need no rules of their own. (a) would repeat the tab bar's rules in a second place, where they could drift apart. (b) cannot tell which tabs are shown, so it would send users to pages they cannot open, or have to look at the tab bar anyway. On a narrow window, tabs that no longer fit move into the "more" menu but stay on the page, so their shortcuts keep working (AC5).
     9	**Consequences:** A `g` shortcut for another tab later takes a few attributes on its link. Each shortcut's description is given separately, because a tab's text also holds its open count. The bell is in the HTML twice, once for small screens and once for large ones, so only one copy declares `g n`, or the two would clash. `g c` carries its own address, because following the Code tab would keep the user on the branch they are browsing (AC2).
    10	
    11	### Decisions for Commit 4
    12	#### Decision 2: `g n` is listed under a new "General" heading shared with the help dialog
    13	
    14	**Decision:** `g n` is listed as "Notifications" under a new "General" heading, kept as a new translated string that will be used by #57 as well.
    15	**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Reuse an existing "General" string, such as the one on the settings pages. (b) List `g n` with no heading, and let the help dialog decide where shortcuts without one go.
    16	**Rationale:** (a) needs no new string, but borrows text translators wrote for the settings pages, so a language that words that tab differently would carry it into the shortcut list. (b) needs no new string either, but `?` would be under "General" while `g n` had no heading, so the dialog would need a rule its spec does not state, and "the site-wide section" in AC8 would come down to interpretation. A shared string gives one heading and one translation, and the list of shortcuts itself says that `g n` and `?` belong together.
    17	**Consequences:** #58 adds one new string for #57 to reuse, so it adds a small hurdle of communication to ensure one's changes do not compete with another's. Shortcuts that work on every page now have a heading to go under.

import {registerGlobalInitFunc} from './observer.ts';
import {hideElem, toggleElem} from '../utils/dom.ts';

const sequenceTimeoutMs = 1500; // the longest wait between the keys of a sequence

export type Shortcut = {
  keys: string, // keys pressed one after another, separated by spaces, e.g. "g c"
  description: string, // translated
  section?: string, // translated
  element?: HTMLElement, // the shortcut only exists while this element is in the document
  action: () => void,
};

export type ShortcutInfo = Pick<Shortcut, 'keys' | 'description' | 'section'>;

function isActive(shortcut: Shortcut): boolean {
  return !shortcut.element || shortcut.element.isConnected;
}

// returns the shortcut for exactly these keys, 'prefix' if they start a longer sequence, or null
function matchKeys(shortcuts: Shortcut[], keys: string): Shortcut | 'prefix' | null {
  for (const shortcut of shortcuts) {
    if (shortcut.keys === keys) return shortcut;
    if (shortcut.keys.startsWith(`${keys} `)) return 'prefix';
  }
  return null;
}

export class ShortcutRegistry {
  shortcuts: Shortcut[] = [];
  pendingKeys = ''; // the start of a sequence pressed so far
  pendingTime = 0;

  register(shortcut: Shortcut) {
    const keys = shortcut.keys.toLowerCase();
    // a shortcut whose element has left the page, e.g. a hint replaced by file tree navigation, gives way to the new one
    this.shortcuts = this.shortcuts.filter(isActive);
    const conflict = this.shortcuts.find((s) => s.keys === keys || s.keys.startsWith(`${keys} `) || keys.startsWith(`${s.keys} `));
    if (conflict) throw new Error(`Keyboard shortcut "${keys}" conflicts with "${conflict.keys}"`);
    this.shortcuts.push({...shortcut, keys});

## Design

Design decisions noted under issue #58.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- `g n` and the tabs in the "more" menu rely on #56 counting a hidden element as present. The bell that declares `g n` is the phone-layout copy, which is hidden on desktops, and tabs in the closed "more" menu are hidden too. If the registry ever started ignoring hidden elements, as #56's Tech Debt suggests later shortcuts might need, both would stop working. The Playwright tests for AC5 and AC6 fail if that happens.

**Encountered:**
- The navbar renders its icons, the notifications bell among them, twice: once for the phone layout and once for desktop, with CSS hiding one. Both copies are always in the page, so marking both with `g n` makes #56's registry throw a clash on every page for signed-in users. Handled by a `WithShortcut` flag that only the copy rendered for every signed-in user passes. The core issue of two notification bells was not fixed here.

## Implementation Note
Despite the changes impacting the user-facing experience, there are no UI changes that require before and after screenshots. As confusing as this may be, these shortcuts only take the user to another page, and don't add, remove or change any element on the page.

## AI assistance

Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) drafted the code, tests, docs and other changes, and ran the headless-browser checks and the checks that each test fails when its code is broken. I made the decisions, refused to let Claude commit on my behalf, and made commits as small as possible so I could review each one with its tests. AI-Log reference under related Issue #58.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-20 00:50:54Z)**_

Cherry-picking won't make a weird history, and it's easier than retyping.

**Why the history stays clean:**
- The sandbox commits were never on a branch and never pushed, so nothing anywhere refers to them.
- Cherry-picking creates brand-new commits on `feat/issue-58-g-shortcuts` with the same changes. On GitHub they look exactly as if you'd typed them there.
- #96 went in as a merge commit (`471077b005`), so your branch already has the #56 code, including your review fix, and the patches apply on top of it. I dry-ran exactly that yesterday.

Plain `git cherry-pick` copies two things you might not want: the original author date (Oct 18) and the original messages, slips included. So I'd use **`git cherry-pick -n <sha>`, one commit at a time**:
- It applies the change and stages it, but doesn't commit.
- You review `git diff --staged`, then `git commit` with your own message, dated today. Same rhythm as before: you make every commit.
- Don't pass several SHAs to one `-n`, because they'd land as one combined change.

In order:

| # | Command | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `git cherry-pick -n cc44473eb5` | link shortcut code + unit tests |
| 2 | `git cherry-pick -n 77f0e39ce9` | `g i/p/a/w` tabs |
| 3 | `git cherry-pick -n df44e52bab` | `g c` |
| 4 | `git cherry-pick -n feedcd50a8` | `g n` + `shortcuts.general` |
| 5 | `git cherry-pick -n 054ea4c2b3` | Playwright tests (fix the missing space before `(#58)`) |
| 6 | `git cherry-pick -n 6a806651fd` | docs, plus two fixes before committing (below) |

Before committing step 6:
- **The guide wording fix from the review.** You never committed it in the sandbox; it's still an uncommitted change there. Since the docs go in one commit anyway, fold it in with `git -C .specstory/sim-58 diff | git apply`. Then the wrong wording never lands at all.
- **`verified-at` and `source-hash`** must point at the real branch, not the sandbox hash. I can make those two edits for you at that point.

If you want, I can run each `-n` step and stop for you to review and commit, exactly as in the sandbox. A cherry-pick with `-n` never commits, so that stays within your rule.
